title: The mud mosque of Djenné
hook: the Great Mosque of mud, replastered by the whole town

segments.voice: Yesterday, Timbuktu's manuscripts, books that sold for more than other goods in the market. Your line was: the city of manuscripts. What did you write by hand? Day nine hundred seventy-one.

Before dawn, drums. Then people pour into the square: boys with baskets of wet mud on their heads, women and girls carrying water from the river, old men giving orders, masons up on the walls. Bundles of palm wood stick out of the building like the bristles of a brush, and men climb them like ladders, smoothing fresh mud over the walls with their hands. By the end of the day a whole mosque has a new skin. This is Djenné, an old town on a river in Mali, and its Great Mosque is built of earth. Today: the mud mosque of Djenné.
screen: `DRUMS BEFORE DAWN.` → `BASKETS OF WET MUD.` → `A WHOLE MOSQUE GETS A NEW SKIN.`

segments.voice: Mud is a strange thing to build a great mosque from. Sun-dried bricks, held together and coated with more mud, mixed with things like rice husks so it holds. It is cool inside in the heat. But mud has an enemy: rain. The rainy season washes some of the walls away. So, by long custom, the town comes out together and puts it back. The masons lead; their skill is handed down in families. Everyone else carries. That bundle of palm sticks poking out of the walls is not decoration. It is scaffolding that never comes down. The chronicler al-Sa'di tells how the town's first mosque came to be: a ruler of Djenné became Muslim, tore down his own palace, and built a mosque on the site. The building that stands today is not that first one, but it stands in its line. The Qur'an has a line about who looks after the houses of God. In Pickthall's translation: "He only shall tend Allah's sanctuaries who believeth in Allah and the Last Day." And a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says that whoever builds a mosque for God, God builds the like of it for them in Paradise. In Djenné, building is never finished. The mosque would melt without the town, and the town gathers because of the mosque. Nobody owns the job. Everyone owns a basket.
screen: `SUN-DRIED BRICK, COATED IN MUD.` · `THE RAINS WASH THE WALLS AWAY.` · `A PALACE TORN DOWN FOR A MOSQUE.` · `THE MOSQUE WOULD MELT WITHOUT THE TOWN.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE TOWN REPLASTERS.`

segments.voice: The practice: repair something together. Settle, and breathe. Think of something shared that is wearing thin. A fence between neighbors. A family tradition nobody has organized lately. A friendship that needs a visit. A room at your mosque, church or community center that needs a coat of paint. Ask who else cares about it, and what one basket of mud you could carry. Hold those people in mind. If you pray, you can ask God's blessing on the work. If you don't, simply picture it finished. The bell holds the time.
The mud mosque of Djenné. The Great Mosque of earth in Mali, washed by the rains and replastered by its town. Today's word.

notes: The index hook says 'every year'; under the claims rule the script says 'by long custom' and ties it to the rainy season. Confirm the replastering is annual and how it is organized today (the masons' guild, roles of young people and women).
Drums before dawn, the race with baskets of mud, rice husks in the mix: widely described features of the festival, without a cited text; confirm or trim.
Al-Sa'di's account of Koi Konboro converting, demolishing his palace and building the first mosque on the site is paraphrased without naming him; confirm.
'The building that stands today is not that first one' (the present mosque was rebuilt in the early twentieth century) is stated without a date; confirm.
Sahih al-Bukhari 450 cited for the hadith on building a mosque; confirm the number.
Pickthall 9:18 quoted (partial verse) from memory; confirm wording.
The practice uses 'picture it finished' (not a hook opening); fine under the rules, but flagging.
Original 'masjid' gloss 'place of prostration' is the common Arabic sense from s-j-d; confirm.
Editor: corrected the review line, which said books were 'worth more than gold'; Leo Africanus says only that they sold for more than other merchandise.
Audit: Bukhari 450's wording is that God builds 'the like of it' in Paradise (the 'house' wording is Muslim's version); the voice and trapdoor now follow Bukhari, which is the cited collection.
